summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated US territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Since the January 2025 executive order, all US identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth, the X marker has been removed from new and renewed passports, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid only until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. A trans visitor arriving on US documents faces that mismatch at the airport, where screening follows US federal procedure.

The same January 2025 order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities used in accordance with their gender identity. The territory's hospital is federally funded, and the January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches it, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed.

Executive Order 14201 restricts trans participation in women's sport, and in February 2025 the State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for that purpose, with an internal SWS25 marking applied to such applicants. The measure reaches US territories through federal agencies, as do the document, facility and care-funding orders.

Partner recognition is unsettled in practice. In July 2015 American Samoa was the only US territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was "still being reviewed... I don't know", while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it, and no licence applications had been made. In January 2016 the territory's incoming District Court judge told his confirmation hearing that he had not read the Supreme Court decision and that the district court "doesn't deal with this ruling", and said he would not perform same-sex weddings absent a change in local law. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no couple has yet applied; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and then the US Department of the Interior. A July 2024 on-island survey still treats the territory's statutory ban as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act of 13 December 2022 obliged recognition of marriages lawfully performed elsewhere.

Local cultural context runs against the federal posture. Fa'afafine, described in a maintained University of Hawai'i at Mānoa research guide as people born male who embody both male and female traits and as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, are organised locally: the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride. A 2009 travel column reported homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, alongside an expectation of reserved behaviour in public by people of all orientations.

Documented incidents involving trans residents indicate real exposure. In September 2023 the US Department of Justice secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.
tangentialFactors:
American Samoa's divergence from peer jurisdictions is the recurring pattern in the marriage record. In 2015 it was the only US territory that had not moved to apply the federal marriage ruling, and in 2016 its judiciary was still operating on the premise that the ruling did not apply automatically, while other outlying jurisdictions had already conformed. The 2026 legal analysis reaching the opposite conclusion has not been tested in court.

The territory declined a formal ban before the point was settled nationally: the Fono Senate voted down a bill outlawing same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. The sponsor framed the bill as pre-emptive against the marriage litigation then unfolding in US states.

Cultural recognition of fa'afafine coexists with a legal and administrative apparatus set in Washington. A visitor's practical exposure is governed by federal document, facility, care and visa policy, while the social environment is described in the sources as one in which a third-gender identity is culturally legible and publicly visible.

Federal litigation over the passport policy was live as of March 2025, so the document posture for trans travellers was contested in court rather than settled, and existing X-marker passports continued to be honoured until expiry.

Accommodation in the territory skews toward business travel in Pago Pago, which bears on where a trans visitor is likely to be staying and how visible they are likely to be.
localsOnly:
Fa'afafine residents have spoken for themselves on the marriage question. At the 2003 committee hearing on the proposed ban, Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not believe in marriages with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, and citing a Christian upbringing.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010 from the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, frames fa'afafine as an integral part of traditional Samoan culture and organises around cultural pride, within a wider account of colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Residents are covered by federal employment machinery. The September 2023 Justice Department settlement with the American Samoa Government resolved an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government over her gender identity.

Marriage for residents remains practically untested: no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory, so the registrar has never been put to the obligation the 2026 analysis describes, and the route to a definitive ruling runs through the High Court of American Samoa and then the US Department of the Interior.

Local expectations of reserved public behaviour apply to residents and visitors alike, regardless of orientation, within a chiefly fa'amatai social structure shared across the two Samoan nations.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling is operative in American Samoa is unresolved in the sources: a 2026 legal analysis says it is, the territory's own officials have said otherwise, and no test case has been brought. The statutory ban is treated as operative on-island as of July 2024.

Whether passports carrying an X marker, or documents whose gender marker does not match presentation, are accepted without incident at American Samoa's ports of entry is not sourced. The federal document rules are documented; their application at this territory's airport is inferred from federal procedure rather than reported.

Enforcement of the January 2025 facility restriction at the territory's federally funded hospital, and of the care-funding order in practice during a visit, is not sourced. The orders are documented; local implementation is not.

Whether American Samoa has its own territorial non-discrimination statute covering gender identity, as distinct from the federal cases described here, is not sourced.

The SWS25 visa marking and the February 2025 announcement of visa denials for trans athletes are documented at national level; no territory-specific application of that policy is sourced.
